$comment: Conformance vectors for docs/TRUST-MODEL.md. Every implementation of the trust
model runs these; whichever side disagrees is the wrong one.
`expected` is the result of preflight ALONE: 'allow', 'deny', or 'ask' meaning the
policy has no answer and a human must be asked. 'ask' is a real outcome and not a
placeholder — an implementation that resolves it early is broken even if the final
Cases are chosen for where a wrong implementation still looks plausible. A vector
may only change when the behaviour is meant to change, never to make a build pass.

cases.name: a read is allowed without asking
cases.why: Rank 0 and non-mutating. It is still a disclosure, which is why it is its own risk and can be refused by rule.

cases.name: a network read is allowed without asking
cases.why: Rank 0 like read, but a distinct risk so a deployment can refuse one without the other.

cases.name: a write asks by default
cases.why: The default posture prompts rather than allowing or refusing. Neither extreme is a safe default.

cases.name: a write is allowed when writes are allowed
execute is refused until explicitly enabled
cases.why: Not 'ask'. Shell access is off, and a prompt would let one keystroke turn it on.

cases.name: execute asks once enabled
cases.why: Enabling execution removes the hard refusal; it does not remove the prompt.

cases.name: read_only refuses every mutation
cases.why: allow_writes is set and loses. A hard refusal is not a preference to be weighed.

cases.name: read_only still permits reads
a session grant does not survive a hard refusal
cases.why: The central ordering property. A grant for writes must never become a grant for execution, and read_only must not be reversible by anything a user clicked earlier.

cases.name: an explicit rule outranks a session grant
cases.why: A rule is the deployment's stated policy; a grant is one person's convenience during one session.

cases.name: a deny_always grant outranks a permissive configuration
cases.why: allow_writes is set. A grant the user gave is consulted before the standing config, so their 'no' holds.

cases.name: a grant is keyed by directory, not by file
cases.why: Approving one write into a directory covers the rest of it. Prompting per file is what makes people approve without reading.

cases.name: a grant does not leak into a sibling directory
cases.why: The other half of the same rule. Directory-scoped, not workspace-scoped.

cases.name: a grant does not leak across tools
a pathless request is keyed by tool alone
a rule matching tool but not path does not fire
cases.why: A rule with a path glob is scoped by it. Matching on tool alone would silently widen every scoped rule.

cases.name: a rule matching both tool and path fires
a tool glob matches a family of tools
the first matching rule wins
cases.why: Order is part of the policy. A later, broader rule must not override an earlier, narrower one.

cases.name: a rule can allow execution that configuration refuses — and loses
cases.why: Hard refusals precede rules. Execution being off is not a default a rule may edit; it is a posture the operator set on the command line.

$comment: Workspace-level, not policy-level: these are refused before any prompt, for READS
as well as writes, and are omitted from listings entirely. A user cannot consent to
a disclosure they have not been shown.
